newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire refugee airlift could take 10 days to start.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugee airlift could take 10 days to start.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Tuesday preparations could take 10 days before an airlift home begins for 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire.
Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said the first to be flown out would be children followed by adults healthy enough to travel.

"It's still going to take a week or 10 days before the start of the airlift. In the meantime we will care for the refugees," said Stromberg, adding fuel shortages both in Kisangani and the east Zairean border city of Goma were slowing the operation.
"The planes will require fuel and the whole logistical operation to be in place before the airlift starts," he said.
"We need planes, a way to add to the transport across the river to bring the refugees up to Kisangani and then simply more trucks as the train is irregular at best," the spokesman added.
U.N. officials, and Stromberg, had said they hoped to start the airlift, one of the largest ever of refugees, this week. UNHCR flew 300 Zairean displaced back to Goma from Kisangani on Monday.
Stromberg said UNHCR was still waiting to hear if Rwanda's government would let the planes fly to Rwanda and first flights might be to Goma or the Zairean town of Bukavu to the south.
Many of the Hutu refugees, who ended up south of Kisangani after six months of fleeing Tutsi-dominated rebels, are from southwestern Rwanda, adjacent to Bukavu. They left Rwanda in 1994.

Rwanda has yet to confirm it will let planes fly refugees straight back to the capital, Kigali. Rwandan-backed rebels now controlling more than a third of Zaire also have concerns about the operation, which they agreed to last weekend.
Stromberg said 96 refugees died on Monday from sickness and malnutrition among 80,000 refugees at two main sites south of Kisangani and 2,716 severely malnourished had been registered.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said it would contribute a C-130 and two Ilyushin-76 transport planes to the airlift and they could repatriate up to 500 refugees per day.
A WFP spokeswoman in Nairobi said the three planes would fly food from Uganda and Tanzania into Kisangani and refugees out.
Stromberg said Zaireans looted a WFP truck loaded with biscuits and therapeutic milk on Monday on the western bank of the Zaire river but feeding continued on Tuesday.
WFP said trucks for the first time were distributing food to the refugees on Tuesday in addition to a train, meaning the refugees could receive a 40 percent heavier ration.
On Saturday, after 48 hours of high-level international pressure, the U.N. extracted an agreement from rebel leader Laurent Kabila to allow the refugees to fly home via Kisangani.

Rwandan authorities will closely screen returnees, the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled into exile in 1994. Many had joined Rwanda's former Hutu army and Interahamwe militia in the genocide of some 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus three years ago.
The rebels want refugees kept in the bush along a rail track south of Kisangani and brought up in batches by truck and by ferry over the Zaire river, renamed the Congo by the rebels.

The rebels seized Kisangani on March 15 and at first refused to allow the Hutu refugees into the city, even in transit. But they backed down with refugees reportedly dying at an average rate of 120 a day.
